transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-04
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Olivia Chen (AE), Marcus Hale (SE) — Redwood; Ravi Patel (Eng Mgr), Sara Gomez (Backend), Tom Li (DevOps), Amira Hassan (Security) — Penguin Labs
Recording: auto
Notes/links mentioned: Quickstart repo: https://bit.ly/rw-quickstart-sdks ; Security pack: https://redwood.example.com/security-pack ; Deck: https://bit.ly/rw-sdk-deck

Summary: Rapid walkthrough of Redwood SDKs (Python + TypeScript), authentication approaches (API key vs SSO/SAML), environment setup for sandbox and CI, and quick configuration recommendations from Optimize. Customer is evaluating hosted vs Dedicated; primary concerns are VPC peering, secret rotation, and SOC2 artifacts.

[00:00] Olivia: Ok hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Olivia from Redwood, and with me is Marcus who'll go into the SDK and infra details. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Ravi: Hey, good thanks. Busy week but excited to get this rolling.
[00:12] Sara: Hi all.
[00:13] Tom: Hey.
[00:15] Amira: Good afternoon.

[00:20] Olivia: Great. Quick agenda: we'll do a 10‑minute orientation on the SDKs and quickstart, Marcus will demo Python and TypeScript snippets, we'll talk auth and best practices for secrets/CI, then leave time for security questions and next steps. Sound ok?
[00:32] Ravi: Yeah sounds good. We're mostly scoped for an MVP — user-facing assistant in our customer portal — so the priorities are latency under 700ms tail for short prompts, cost control, and keeping PII off platform where needed.

[00:50] Marcus: Cool. I'll start with the repo and local env. So quick note: we have two official SDKs — python and typescript — both wrap the same Redwood REST/streaming endpoints. The quickstart repo has a minimal flask/express example, env var pattern, and a CI snippet for GitHub Actions.
[01:10] Marcus: (screen-share) opening the repo now — file tree: examples/python/quickstart.py, examples/ts/quickstart.ts, .env.example, ci/workflows/redwood-ci.yml. For local dev we recommend REDWOOD_API_KEY set in your shell or a .env injected by your secret manager.
[01:30] Sara: Are those API keys scoped per route or global? We rotate keys daily for some services.
[01:36] Marcus: Keys are project-scoped by default, and you can create scoped tokens in the console for read-only or limited usage. We also support SSO/SAML for the console and team access, plus short-lived per-host tokens if you want ephemeral secrets tied to a backend identity provider.
[01:52] Olivia: We usually recommend service-level API keys for backend-to-backend calls, and ephemeral tokens for client devices.

[02:05] Marcus: Now the python snippet.
[02:10] Marcus: "from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY'])
resp = client.text.generate(model='redwood-3b', prompt='Summarize...')" — that's the minimal flow. The SDK handles streaming and retry logic; you can enable streaming with "stream=True".
[02:35] Ravi: redwood-3b — is that quantized or full fp? What's the latency profile?
[02:42] Marcus: For small models we have quantized variants — we call them like redwood-3b-q4 — they trade a bit of quality for 2-3x cost improvement. For your latency target I'd recommend the standard 3b in Hosted for the initial pilot; if cost becomes an issue we can suggest a q4 variant or batching/kv cache. We have benchmarks in the deck.

[03:05] [Crosstalk]
[03:06] Sara: And for embeddings — any differences in SDK usage?
[03:09] Marcus: Embeddings are separate endpoints: client.embeddings.create(...). The SDK returns numpy arrays in Python and float32 arrays in TS. Small note: for embeddings we recommend async batching on the client if you have high throughput.

[03:25] Marcus: Quick TS example: "import Redwood from '@redwood-ai/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const out = await client.text.generate({model: 'redwood-3b', prompt: '...'});" It's intentionally close to the REST payload so switching between languages is trivial.

[03:50] Ravi: Cool. Now on env / CI: we run everything through GitHub Actions and use Vault for secrets. We need to make sure keys never leak to client bundles. Any best practices?
[04:01] Marcus: Absolutely. Server-side only. Put keys in Vault, inject in CI as environment secrets only for deploy jobs. The quickstart has a workflow snippet that shows how to call the SDK in a deploy step, and we recommend using ephemeral task tokens for any ephemeral build agents.
[04:18] Marcus: Also, avoid running long-lived API keys in browser JS. For client features, use a proxy endpoint which mints ephemeral tokens via the SDK.

[04:30] Tom: For our security folks — what about KMS? We use AWS KMS to encrypt secrets. How does Redwood handle encryption at rest / key management?
[04:40] Amira: (asks) Is there an HSM integration?
[04:42] Olivia: Short answer: hosted Redwood encrypts at rest; customers can integrate with their KMS/HSM for Private deployments. We have two patterns: Hosted with Redwood-managed keys and Private with customer-managed KMS. For SOC2 scope we can provide the security pack and an architecture note.
[04:58] Marcus: I'll drop the security doc after the call. The security pack includes our encryption details, rotation policy, and sample SOC2 artifacts.

[05:10] Ravi: Great. About VPC peering — we may need a dedicated instance with VPC peering for the pilot. Can you explain Dedicated vs Hosted and the networking options?
[05:22] Marcus: Sure. Hosted is quickest, traffic goes over TLS to our edge; Dedicated gives you a reserved GPU pool with VPC peering and private endpoints. With Dedicated we can peer or set up private connectivity and also pin model versions. For some regulated flows, Private (VPC + customer KMS) is the right fit.
[05:41] Tom: For VPC peering we need IP ranges and a plan for NAT/egress. What's the standard?
[05:47] Olivia: Typical flow: we provide a small list of CIDRs we use for peering, you add them to your routing table, and we validate with a handshake. We'll collect the exact ranges in the follow-up.

[06:02] Marcus: Back to SDKs — let's demo a small dev flow that includes caching. If you have repetitive prompts the SDK can include a prefix cache via KV to reduce token count. In Python it's a config flag: client.config.cache = True, cache_backend='redis'. That reduces token cost for repeated system prompts or shared context.
[06:25] Sara: Could you explain KV cache — is that different from model key-value cache?
[06:29] Marcus: Good question. There's two things: the runtime-level KV cache (for transformer key/value tensors during decoding) — that's not something you control directly — and the application-level prefix cache where you store previous responses or partial contexts in Redis. We call that prefix/KV cache in docs which sometimes leads to confusion; sorry for the naming.

[06:48] Amira: (typing) noted.

[07:00] Marcus: Now a short walk through error handling and retries. The SDK will surface 429s and there's a built-in exponential backoff; but for UI flows we recommend client-side cancels at ~3s and server retries up to 5s depending on your latency budget.
[07:18] Ravi: Our app cares a lot about tail latency — 95th at 700ms — what's typical?
[07:23] Marcus: For short prompts on a single-token-ish response the hosted 3b median is ~120ms but tail varies. We'll need to run your actual payload; that's why Marcus will run the perf test with your sample dataset.

[07:40] Olivia: I want to flag Optimize — it's a consultant-style toolkit and in-console suggestions we can enable. It looks at token distribution and suggests batching sizes, quantization profiles, and cache recommendations. That tends to give a 20–40% cost win without hurting quality.
[07:58] Sara: Is Optimize an extra cost?
[08:01] Olivia: It's part of the platform — some advanced features are in higher tiers; we'll share the specific pricing items in the follow-up.

[08:10] Marcus: Ok jumping back to code: demoing streaming in TS — small snippet shows handling partial chunks and rendering to a web socket in a frontend. (reads code) handleDelta(chunk) { ... } — we also have server-side SSE examples.
[08:28] Tom: Any CORS implications if we do a frontend-only implementation?
[08:32] Marcus: You can't expose server API keys in the browser. If you must have direct browser calls, use ephemeral tokens minted by your backend which are restricted in scope and TTL.

[08:45] [15s pause — screen-share switching]

[09:05] Olivia: Security deep dive — Amira, are there specific compliance questions you want us to answer now, or should we collect them and follow up?
[09:12] Amira: We have a list but main points: SOC2, encryption at rest and in transit, RBAC for console, audit logs retention, and data residency. Also we need proof of penetration testing cadence.

[09:26] Marcus: For hosted, TLS in transit is standard, logs are available in the Console for up to 90 days depending on plan; RBAC is SSO-based with role tiers. For Private deployments, logs can be exported to your SIEM and retention is configurable. Pen tests are annual; we can share redacted reports.

[09:50] Amira: Good. Send the SOC2 + pen test summary.
[09:54] Olivia: Will do.

[10:00] Marcus: Now a short failure scenario: if a model variant is out of capacity, we have smart routing and fallback to compatible variants — you can configure fallback chains per route in the Console. That avoids 503s in many cases.
[10:18] Ravi: Nice. Does the SDK surface cost estimates per call?
[10:22] Marcus: We return token counts in the response meta; we also expose a cost estimator locally. The Console gives token-level cost breakdowns by route and model.

[10:35] Sara: Regarding secret rotation in CI — we use ephemeral deploy tokens and rotate daily. Any gotchas?
[10:42] Marcus: Make sure the token lifetime matches your deploy window; if you rotate mid-deploy you'll see failures. We advise a short TTL for ephemeral tokens but not shorter than your longest job duration. For long-running batch jobs, use a service account pattern with automatic rotation.

[10:58] Tom: On the network side, does Dedicated require egress through Redwood NAT? We need to enforce internal egress filters.
[11:05] Marcus: For Dedicated you can keep egress inside the peered link; we support routing rules so egress traffic can be controlled. We'll capture the specifics after you share CIDRs.

[11:20] Olivia: I'm going to demo the quickstart in a tiny live run — Marcus will trigger the sample requests and we'll watch the Console.
[11:28] Marcus: (runs python quickstart) Starting with REDWOOD_API_KEY set, running quickstart generate... streaming comes through.
[11:35] [00:11:35] Marcus: See the Console trace? It logs the route, token counts, and latency. Here you can click into per-token breakdown and see model variant and which kernel was used — that's the kernel selection telemetry we surface.
[11:52] Sara: I see the trace — cool. That token break down is helpful.

[12:05] Marcus: Small caveat: the telemetry naming from our infra sometimes shows internal node names; we've a mapping file for friendly node names — we'll include that in the follow-up.

[12:18] Ravi: About billing: if we start with Hosted and then move to Dedicated, how does that transition work? Do we get credits?
[12:27] Olivia: Transition is usually contractual — we can apply usage credits or migration discounts as part of a Dedicated contract; that goes through our sales ops. I'll include a draft pricing sheet.

[12:40] [Short pause — people typing]

[12:50] Marcus: Ok now let's talk about local dev and reproducibility — we recommend the docker-compose in examples to emulate the runtime client, plus a small wrapper that records tokenized prompts so your CI can run deterministic checks.
[13:07] Sara: Deterministic tests — is that for QA?
[13:10] Marcus: Yes, snapshot tests against outputs, but caution: non-deterministic models will drift; so we suggest tolerance thresholds and golden prompt sets for important flows. Redwood Optimize can hook up to those evals and alert on regressions.

[13:30] Ravi: For the pilot timeline, we want sandbox by next Tuesday and a perf readout by two weeks after. Is that feasible?
[13:38] Olivia: Yes, sandbox next Tuesday (2025-08-06) should be fine — I'll send keys today. Perf by 2025-08-18 is doable; Marcus will coordinate.

[13:47] Amira: About data residency — some of our customers are EU-only; do you support region pinning?
[13:55] Marcus: Yes, we have region pins for models and data. Hosted regions include us-west, eu-west, and ap-southeast. Private can be fully on-prem. We'll include region specifics in the follow-up.

[14:10] Sara: Any gotchas integrating with Next.js SSR and Redwood SDK?
[14:15] Marcus: Server-side rendered pages are fine if you never expose keys to the client. Use getServerSideProps to call the SDK and render results. If you need streaming to the browser, use a server proxy or SSE channel.

[14:30] [longer demo step — Marcus executes TS quickstart and shows streaming on the frontend sample]

[15:05] Tom: For our CI pipeline, we run integration tests in a build matrix — will we hit rate limits?
[15:12] Marcus: The default rate limits are tiered; for pilot workloads test will probably be fine. If you expect concurrent matrix runs you can request higher rate limits or provision Dedicated capacity.

[15:25] Ravi: Can you talk briefly about SSO onboarding? We use Okta.
[15:29] Olivia: Okta is supported out of the box. You can flip SSO in the Console, map groups to roles, and then we provision team members via SAML assertion. For API access you can tie team service accounts to Okta apps for provisioning short-lived tokens.

[15:46] Amira: And audit logs retention? We need 1 year retention for some projects.
[15:51] Marcus: By default hosted retention is 90 days, enterprise plans can extend to 365 days and stream logs to your SIEM. For Private you control retention fully.

[16:05] Sara: Any resource recommendations for testing batching?
[16:09] Marcus: Use the perf tool in the repo; it simulates concurrent requests and variable prompt lengths. We'll run it with your sample payloads.

[16:18] Marcus: Quick note on tokens and cost: short system prompts add up. Use prefix caching for system messages and compress prompts where possible. Optimize shows hot prompts and token medians.

[16:35] Ravi: Are there SDK hooks for custom telemetry if we want to attach trace ids?
[16:40] Marcus: Yes, there's a request metadata header you can pass like x-redwood-trace-id and we propagate that into Console traces. We'll add that header example to the quickstart.

[16:50] Olivia: We're at security Qs — Amira, anything else?
[16:53] Amira: I'd like the pen test summary, SOC2 docs, and a short blurb about encryption key control in Dedicated vs Hosted. Also who at Redwood signs the DPA? We may need a data processing agreement.

[17:06] Olivia: We'll include DPA routing — usually our legal team sends a standard DPA, happy to work redlines. I'll attach contacts.

[17:16] Sara: Small UX question — do you have rate-limiting headers in responses? We want to surface remaining credits.

[17:21] Marcus: Yes, we return x-rw-remaining, x-rw-limit in responses and you can wire alerts off those values in the Console.

[17:30] Ravi: Ok last bit — can we demo a simple canary deploy? We want to rollout a model change to 10% of traffic and observe metrics.

[17:38] Marcus: Canary is in the Console. You define the rollout rule (percent by route) and we do traffic splitting with automatic rollback on error thresholds. We can also do A/B tests with metric hooks.

[17:52] Olivia: All right, we're coming up on time. Quick recap of next steps: Olivia to send sandbox keys and quickstart links; Marcus to run perf tests; Tom to share network ranges; Amira to collect compliance list. We'll schedule a follow-up week of 2025-08-18 to review perf and Dedicated options.

[18:15] Ravi: Thanks everyone this was super helpful.
[18:18] Sara: Thanks.
[18:19] Tom: Appreciate it.
[18:20] Amira: Thanks.
[18:22] Olivia: Great thanks — we'll follow up in email with the links and action items. Bye for now.

Transcript notes: transcription contains occasional mis-heard terms (internal node names abbreviated, KV cache pronounced K V cash in one spot), filler words, and some overlapping talk. The Console links and quickstart repo referenced above will be sent in the follow-up email.
